title: Report on Studying at the University of Munich
paragraphs: This spring I had a six-week study abroad experience at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) in Munich, Germany. For the first four weeks I took part in the Neurology Winter School, and for the latter two weeks I did an additional clerkship in neurology, so it was six weeks in which I could focus on the field of neuroscience. It was my first study abroad, and I carried great anxiety about whether I could communicate sufficiently in English and whether I could fit in locally. But looking back, helped by many people, including the professors, my family, friends and local companions, I was able to spend very fulfilling and enjoyable days. I would like to look back on this memorable study abroad experience in three parts: the Winter School, the additional clerkship and local life.

The Winter School is a short-term program in which medical students gathered from around the world are paired with LMU students as buddies and take part in ward clerkships at LMU University Hospital (Großhadern) and small-group lectures. The Winter School is divided into Neurology and Oncology, and I took part in the Neurology Winter School with nine other companions. In the morning I did clerkships on the neurology ward. I was assigned to a ward where patients stay for a short time to decide on a treatment plan, and I did procedures such as blood sampling and IV lines and neurological examinations of patients. At that time, my buddy Luisa helped me in many situations, such as translating what patients said from German into English and teaching me how to draw blood. Also, not only Luisa but also the PJ students (sixth-year medical students) on the ward willingly took on translation and assisting with procedures, and thanks to them I could approach the clerkship more eagerly. What I felt at this time was that German medical students did far more work than Japanese medical students, such as writing documents to the hospitals to which patients were referred and writing the senior doctors' examinations in the chart during ward rounds. They were already working like Japanese specialty trainees, and as a fellow medical student I realised that a big gap had opened up and was shocked. Also, through this ward clerkship I could see many diseases I had never experienced in Japan. Experiencing rare diseases such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) associated with immunosuppression after kidney transplantation, HIV-related toxoplasma encephalitis and primary central nervous system lymphoma made my interest in neurology even stronger. A full one-hour lunch break was ensured, and my buddy Luisa taught me that "a break is one of the important jobs, and it is foolish to neglect it." There was a large cafeteria in the hospital, and authentic Bavarian dishes such as crispy roasted meat on the bone were served, and they were truly delicious. In the afternoons, experts in each field related to neuroscience gave lectures on various themes such as vertigo, brain tumors, movement disorders and epilepsy. I heard many interesting things, such as that epilepsy has a premonitory symptom called an aura, that vertical nystagmus strongly suggests a central lesion, and that deep brain stimulation (DBS) is actually not stimulation but inhibition, and I feel that being able to learn about neuroscience so evenly was possible only because of the well-structured program of the Neurology Winter School. Through the lectures I was also greatly stimulated by the eager attitude of my Winter School companions. Every student understood the diseases well, asked questions actively during class and started discussions. In Japan, I think time for questions is often set aside at the end of a lecture and questions come out then, but at the Winter School students asked questions freely whenever they wanted to, and it was attractive that the discussion deepened interactively on the spot. Also, the Winter School was fulfilling not only for the clerkships and lectures but also for the many opportunities to interact with students from around the world. Excursions to nearby towns were also included in the program, and hearing about cultures I did not know there and learning how Japan looks to others was enjoyable and interesting. Above all, I feel that the experience of helping each other and getting through the clerkship with companions of different backgrounds broadened me further.

In the additional clerkship I mainly observed outpatient clinics in neurology. In the initial guidance Prof. Dimitriadis told me I would see the stroke ambulance and the dementia ambulance, and I wondered whether I would be looking at ambulances, and what a dementia ambulance could be, but apparently "Ambulanz" in German means an outpatient department, so I was allowed to see the stroke follow-up clinic and the dementia specialty clinic. In the outpatient clinics, the doctors carefully explained the key points of the examination and, with the patients' cooperation, let me actually perform neurological examinations. At this time, I was impressed that many patients were cooperative with the examination and warmly welcomed a trainee from abroad. The period of the additional clerkship was fulfilling from a different side than the Winter School, and I strongly feel I was right to have requested these two weeks of clerkship. While at the Winter School I could benefit from the best program that had already been prepared, in the additional clerkship the content was left largely to me, and I could freely decide what to observe according to my own wishes. I stayed in the outpatient clinic, joined the ward, observed tests such as EEG and EMG, or visited the epilepsy unit and stroke unit, going freely around the departments I was interested in, and heard the essence of each department from the technicians and doctors working there. In particular, visiting and talking at the epilepsy unit, which I had not seen much of at the Winter School, was impressive, and my sense of weakness regarding epilepsy not only decreased but it suddenly became a field of interest.

What I felt above all in my life there was that I was always having some kind of problem. A bus that departed earlier than the scheduled time, an Airbnb owner who could only communicate in Arabic, a washing machine that kept running for more than three hours: various troubles I had never encountered in Japan were always happening somewhere. I was bewildered for a while, but gradually, by taking the attitude that trouble is bound to happen, I became able to enjoy life including the unexpected. What I especially liked in life there were three things: beer, pretzels and lakes. Perhaps because it is the home of beer, the beer, including that bought at supermarkets, was cheap and delicious. At first I thought pretzels were hard and salty and not tasty, but looking back now I bought and ate them every day. I think that things loved locally surely have a corresponding appeal. As for food, perhaps because it was a short period of six weeks, I rarely missed Japanese food and instead came to like local food such as bread, potatoes and pork more and more. The lakes are Lake Starnberg and Lake Tegernsee, which can be reached in about an hour from the city of Munich, and I felt envious of the environment where quiet nature appears just by going a little away from the city. Regarding Lake Starnberg in particular, it was something Prof. Remi recommended to me in a hospital corridor, saying, "If you come to study in Munich, you should not stay only in the hospital. It is also important to see lakes, mountains and rivers." The lakes and rivers were quiet places where swans swam leisurely and people came to relax after work. I felt that for the people of Munich, having nature nearby is important and a source of peace of mind.

What I learned through this study abroad is that Japanese Silent and Smiling are not virtues abroad. When my life there began, I heard that the characteristics of the Japanese are the 3S (Silent, Smiling, Sleeping), and I vividly remember thinking that this was exactly me, covering up English I could not catch with a polite smile. Depending on the situation, Silent and Smiling may please people as being Japanese-like, but I felt that if you want to learn something abroad or fit in there, you must be more proactive and honest. Until then I had the feeling in myself that if I stayed silent it was zero, and if I said something wrong it was a minus, but I realised that in truth silence is a minus because it is as if showing a lack of interest, and conversely, being able to say something even if you are wrong or imperfect is a plus. Also, when I did not understand the other person's English, I learned that getting by with a polite smile never leads to growth and that it is important to gather courage and ask "Sorry?" From now on, I would like to recognise that Silent and Smiling can take away opportunities for growth, and not forget the self who took on challenges proactively abroad.

Finally, I was able to have such a valuable study abroad experience during my student days thanks to the International Collaboration Office staff, beginning with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, Dr. Itzel, who built up my ability in the medical English class, and the professors of LMU, beginning with Professor Dimitriadis, who planned the wonderful program and accepted me for the additional clerkship. I am convinced that this experience will be a lifelong asset for me. Thank you very much.
